title: The Printing Press
tagline: From clay marks to glowing screens: how words learned to multiply
intro: Imagine a world where every single book had to be copied by hand, letter by letter, taking months of work. For most of human history, that was real life. In this Deep Dive we follow one of the biggest adventures in all of history: how people learned to record words and then copy them fast. We start with clay tablets in ancient Sumer, travel to China where paper and woodblock printing were born, visit Korea where metal type was cast long before Europe, and arrive in Mainz, Germany, where Johannes Gutenberg built a printing system that changed the world. Then we watch printing spread like wildfire, sparking arguments, science, newspapers and revolutions, before steam engines, giant rotary presses, photocopiers, laser printers and the internet take over. Along the way you will learn exactly how the machines work, who deserves the credit, what went wrong, and where printing might go next, even into 3D.

outline.title: Before Books Were Easy
covers: Life before writing: memory, storytellers and oral tradition (songs, epics, family histories passed down by speaking)
Cave paintings and tally marks as early ways of storing information (e.g. Lascaux cave art, about 17,000 years old)
Sumer and the city of Uruk (in today's Iraq): clay tokens for counting goods turn into cuneiform writing around 3300–3200 BCE
How cuneiform worked: a reed stylus pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay; tablets dried in the sun or were baked
Cylinder seals (from about 3500 BCE): carved stone cylinders rolled across clay to make the same picture again and again — an early 'printing-like' idea of repeating an image
Egyptian hieroglyphs (about 3200 BCE) and scribes as a rare, highly trained profession
keyFacts: Cuneiform appeared in Uruk around 3300–3200 BCE and was used for about 3,000 years
Cylinder seals were used in Mesopotamia from about 3500 BCE to sign and seal documents
Many tens of thousands of clay tablets survive, including Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh (600s BCE) — fire baked many tablets harder, helping them survive
outline.hook: Clay was tough but heavy — so people began searching for lighter things to write on and simpler ways to write.

outline.title: Alphabets, Scrolls and the First Books
covers: Papyrus in Egypt: made from strips of the papyrus reed pressed together, rolled into scrolls (papyrus is NOT true paper)
The alphabet: early alphabets (Proto-Sinaitic, about 1800s BCE) led to the Phoenician alphabet (about 1050 BCE), then Greek and Latin — far fewer symbols to learn than cuneiform or hieroglyphs
Parchment and vellum made from animal skins; the legend that parchment was invented at Pergamon when Egypt cut off papyrus (told by Pliny — label as a legend)
The Library of Alexandria (founded about 300 BCE) and copying scrolls by hand
The codex: pages stacked and bound on one side, replacing scrolls between about the 1st and 4th centuries CE
The mysterious Phaistos Disc from Crete (around 1700 BCE, date uncertain) whose symbols were pressed with stamps — a curiosity, not a real printing industry
keyFacts: The Phoenician alphabet had 22 letters, all consonants; the Greeks added vowels
By around 400 CE the codex had largely replaced the scroll for books in the Roman world
A big book on vellum could need the skins of dozens or even hundreds of animals
outline.hook: Scrolls and skins were expensive — but far to the east, someone was about to make a cheap new writing material from plants and rags.

outline.title: The Paper Revolution in China
covers: Writing in early China on bamboo strips, wooden slips and silk — bamboo was heavy and silk expensive
Cai Lun, a Han dynasty court official, presented an improved papermaking method to Emperor He in 105 CE using tree bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets
Older paper fragments found in China (e.g. Fangmatan, about 2nd century BCE) prove paper existed before Cai Lun — he improved and promoted it rather than inventing it from nothing
How paper is made (science, simply): fibers are beaten into a pulp in water, a screen scoops up a thin layer, water drains, fibers tangle and bond as they dry
Why paper was a big deal: light, cheap, smooth, and it takes ink well
Paper spreads within Asia to Korea and Japan (by around the 600s CE)
keyFacts: 105 CE is the traditional date for Cai Lun's report to the emperor
Paper fibers stick together mainly through hydrogen bonds formed as the wet sheet dries
Cai Lun was later honored in China as the patron of papermakers
outline.hook: For centuries papermaking was mostly an Asian skill — until it began travelling west along the Silk Road.

outline.title: Paper Travels the World
covers: Paper reaches Samarkand in Central Asia; the famous story that Chinese prisoners from the Battle of Talas (751) taught papermaking is a traditional tale — historians think paper may have arrived earlier (label as tradition)
Baghdad's paper industry from around 794 under the Abbasid Caliphate (Harun al-Rashid's era); the House of Wisdom and a huge Islamic book culture
Paper in Cairo, North Africa and Muslim Spain — Xàtiva (Játiva) near Valencia was a paper center by the 1100s
Italy: Fabriano becomes a famous papermaking town by the late 1200s, adding water-powered hammer mills, gelatin sizing and watermarks
Watermarks explained: a wire design on the mould makes the paper thinner there, so it shows when held to light
Paper mills spread through Europe in the 1300s, so by 1400 Europe had a cheap surface ready for printing
keyFacts: Baghdad had paper production by around 794–795 CE
The earliest known European watermarks date from the late 1200s in Italy (around 1282)
European paper was made mostly from linen and cotton rags until the 1800s
outline.hook: Paper was spreading everywhere — and in East Asia people had already found a way to stamp whole pages onto it.

outline.title: Woodblocks: Printing a Whole Page at Once
covers: From seals and stone rubbings to woodblock printing in Tang dynasty China (by around the 600s–700s)

How woodblock printing works: text written on thin paper is pasted face-down on a wooden block, the carver cuts away everything except the raised mirror-image characters, then the block is inked and paper is rubbed on top with a brush
Korea's Mugujeonggwang Great Dharani Sutra, found in 1966 inside a pagoda at Bulguksa temple, printed before 751
Japan's Hyakumanto Darani: Empress Shōtoku ordered one million printed Buddhist charms placed in tiny wooden pagodas (about 764–770)

The Diamond Sutra of 868 — the oldest surviving printed book with an exact date — found in 1900 by Wang Yuanlu in a sealed cave at Dunhuang and taken to Britain by Aurel Stein in 1907; now in the British Library
Huge woodblock projects: the Korean Tripitaka Koreana (1200s), over 81,000 blocks still kept at Haeinsa temple
keyFacts: The Diamond Sutra scroll is over 5 meters long and dated to the year 868; its note says Wang Jie had it made for his parents
The Tripitaka Koreana has about 81,000 woodblocks, carved 1237–1248
Woodblock printing is still well suited to Chinese, which uses thousands of different characters
outline.hook: Carving a whole new block for every page was slow — so a clever commoner in China wondered: what if each character was its own tiny piece?

outline.title: Movable Type Is Born in Asia
covers: Bi Sheng invents movable type from baked clay (ceramic) during the 1040s; we know because Shen Kuo described it in his Dream Pool Essays (about 1088)
How Bi Sheng's system worked: characters set in an iron frame on a bed of wax and resin, warmed so type stuck, pressed flat, printed, then melted loose for reuse
Wang Zhen's wooden type (about 1297–1298) — over 60,000 characters arranged on revolving round tables so typesetters could reach them; described in his Nong Shu (1313)

Korea casts metal type: records mention a metal-type book in 1234 (now lost); Jikji, printed at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type (kept in the National Library of France)
King Sejong and the invention of the Hangul alphabet (created 1443, announced 1446) — partly to make reading easier for ordinary people
Why movable type did not instantly take over in China: thousands of characters, plus woodblocks were cheap and flexible
keyFacts: Jikji (1377) is about 78 years older than the Gutenberg Bible and is on UNESCO's Memory of the World register (2001)
Bi Sheng's type dates to the Qingli reign period, 1041–1048
Hangul has 24 basic letters in modern use
outline.hook: Meanwhile, in Europe, books were still being copied by hand — and demand was exploding.

outline.title: Europe's Hand-Copied Books
covers: Monasteries and scriptoria: monks copying books with quills on parchment; illuminated manuscripts with gold and bright colors
The Book of Kells (around 800) as a famous example; one Bible could take a scribe many months to years
Universities (Bologna, Paris, Oxford) create new demand; the pecia system rented out sections of approved texts for students to copy; professional lay scribes and stationers
Rising literacy among merchants and townspeople in the 1300s–1400s, cheap paper arriving, and demand for prayer books (books of hours), schoolbooks and documents
Early European woodcut prints (around 1400s): religious pictures, playing cards, and 'block books' with text and pictures cut on one block
Medieval people were not 'all illiterate' or ignorant — but books were rare and costly
keyFacts: The Book of Kells was made around 800 by monks, probably at Iona and Kells
European block books mostly date from about the 1450s–1470s, around the same time as early type printing
Before 1450 a large library in Europe might hold only a few hundred books
outline.hook: In the German city of Mainz, a goldsmith with big debts and a bigger idea was getting ready to change all of this.

outline.title: Gutenberg's Secret Project
covers: Johannes Gutenberg, born in Mainz around 1400 (exact year unknown) to a well-off family; trained in metalwork
His years in Strasbourg (1430s–1440s): a business making polished metal pilgrim mirrors for the Aachen pilgrimage
The 1439 Strasbourg lawsuit (after partner Andreas Dritzehn died): witnesses mention a press, metal forms and secret work — an early clue to his printing experiments
Return to Mainz around 1448; borrows money, including large loans from the businessman Johann Fust (800 guilders around 1450 and another 800 around 1452)
Why he needed so much money: metal, paper, vellum, workers and years of experiments before any profit
Early small printed items from Mainz: Latin grammar booklets (Donatus) and printed indulgences dated 1454
keyFacts: Gutenberg's birth year is unknown; historians say around 1400 (estimates range about 1394–1404)
Fust lent Gutenberg about 1,600 guilders in total — a huge sum, enough to buy several houses
Printed indulgence certificates from Mainz are dated 1454
outline.hook: Gutenberg's real genius was not one machine but a whole system — starting with a tiny mould that could cast letters perfectly every time.

outline.title: How Gutenberg's System Worked
covers: The punch: a steel rod with a letter carved in mirror image at its tip
The matrix: the punch is struck into softer copper, leaving a letter-shaped dent
The hand mould: an adjustable two-part mould holding the matrix, so thousands of identical letters ('sorts') can be cast quickly with exact height
Type metal: an alloy of lead, tin and antimony — melts at a low temperature, flows into fine detail, and the antimony helps it expand slightly as it cools so letters come out sharp
Oil-based ink (like painters' varnish, with soot) that sticks to metal type, unlike the water-based inks used for woodblocks
The press: adapted from screw presses already used for wine, olive oil and papermaking — Gutenberg combined existing ideas in a new way
Fair credit: the system's big innovation was mass-producing reusable metal type in Europe; Korea had cast metal type earlier but by different methods
keyFacts: The Gutenberg Bible's typeface used around 290 different characters, including joined letters and abbreviations, to imitate handwriting
Lead melts at about 327 °C and tin at about 232 °C; the alloy melts lower than pure lead
Experts estimate around 100,000 pieces of type might be needed for a big job like the Bible
outline.hook: With his system finally working, Gutenberg set out on the most daring project of all: a giant, beautiful Bible.

outline.title: The Gutenberg Bible and a Broken Partnership
covers: The 42-line Bible (named for the lines per column), completed in Mainz around 1454–1455, in two big volumes of about 1,280 pages
Copies on paper and on vellum; red headings and decorations often added by hand afterwards
Enea Silvio Piccolomini (later Pope Pius II) wrote in 1455 that he saw pages in Frankfurt so neat you could read them without glasses
Fust sued Gutenberg in 1455 to get his money back; Fust and Peter Schoeffer (a former scribe in the workshop) took over much of the equipment
Fust and Schoeffer's Mainz Psalter (14 August 1457): the first printed book with a printed date and printers' names, and with printed colored initials
Gutenberg's later years: kept printing on a smaller scale, received a court pension from the Archbishop of Mainz in 1465, died in February 1468, never rich
Rival claim: the Dutch legend that Laurens Janszoon Coster of Haarlem printed first — label as a legend without solid evidence
keyFacts: Estimates say about 160–180 copies were printed; 49 copies (or substantial parts) survive
Roughly three-quarters of the copies were on paper and the rest on vellum
In 1978 a Gutenberg Bible sold for about 2.2 million US dollars; one complete copy is in the Library of Congress
outline.hook: Gutenberg's workshop was the start — but how did a busy print shop actually turn type into pages, day after day?

outline.title: Inside an Early Print Shop
covers: The compositor picks letters from the type case into a composing stick, upside-down and backwards, line by line
Justification: adding spaces so every line is the same width; lines go into a galley, pages are locked into a metal frame (chase) to make a forme
Inking with leather ink balls; paper (often dampened) is placed on the tympan and held by the frisket, slid under the platen, and the pressman pulls the bar
Imposition: arranging pages so that when a big sheet is folded it reads in order — folio, quarto, octavo
Words that came from print shops: 'upper case' and 'lower case' from where capital and small letters were kept in the type cases
Teams of workers: compositors, pressmen, apprentices; proofreaders checking errors; type was distributed back into the cases after printing
The wooden hand press barely changed for about 350 years
keyFacts: A two-person press crew could print roughly 200–250 sheets on one side per hour
In an octavo, one big sheet folded three times makes 8 leaves (16 pages)
'Upper case' and 'lower case' come from the positions of the type cases on the compositor's stand
outline.hook: Print shops did not stay in Mainz for long — and a war in 1462 helped scatter printers across Europe.

outline.title: Printing Spreads Like Wildfire
covers: The sack of Mainz in 1462 scatters printers; presses open in Subiaco and Rome (Sweynheym and Pannartz, 1465), Venice (1469), Paris (1470) and many more towns
Venice becomes Europe's printing capital; Nicolas Jenson's beautiful roman type (1470)
Aldus Manutius and the Aldine Press: small, portable octavo books and the first italic type (1501, cut by Francesco Griffo)

William Caxton prints the first book in English (Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, Bruges, about 1473–1474) and sets up England's first press in Westminster in 1476, printing Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
Incunabula: books printed before 1501
Book prices fall dramatically, and many more kinds of books appear: grammars, travel tales, calendars, medical and legal books
keyFacts: By 1500 printing presses were working in more than 250 European towns
Around 30,000 different editions of incunabula are known; estimates of total copies range roughly from 8 to 20 million
Caxton's press in Westminster started in 1476
outline.hook: Cheap, fast printing meant new ideas could now spread faster than anyone could stop them — and an angry monk was about to prove it.

outline.title: Ideas Unleashed: Reformation and Science
covers: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517) are printed and spread across Germany within weeks; pamphlets and woodcut cartoons argue both sides
Luther's German New Testament (1522) and William Tyndale's English New Testament (1526, printed in Worms) bring the Bible to ordinary readers
The Catholic Church and rulers respond with censorship, licensing and the Index of Prohibited Books (1559)
Science: identical printed copies with accurate pictures let scholars check, compare and correct each other — Copernicus's On the Revolutions and Vesalius's Fabrica (both 1543)
Printed maps, tables and diagrams improve navigation and mathematics
Historian Elizabeth Eisenstein's idea (1979) that print was an 'agent of change' — and fair debate about how much print alone caused
keyFacts: Luther's writings made up a very large share of all printing in Germany in the early 1520s
Copernicus's book was published in 1543, the year he died
The Index of Prohibited Books lasted until 1966
outline.hook: Printing was changing religion and science — next it would change everyday life with news, spelling, and print shops across the globe.

outline.title: News, Spelling and Print Around the World
covers: The first newspapers: Johann Carolus's 'Relation' in Strasbourg (1605); the first English daily, the Daily Courant (1702)
Almanacs, broadsides, ballads and posters; Benjamin Franklin as a printer and publisher (Poor Richard's Almanack, 1732–1758)
Standardized spelling and dictionaries, e.g. Samuel Johnson's Dictionary (1755); more people learn to read
Copyright begins: Britain's Statute of Anne (1710) gives authors rights for a limited time
Printing reaches the world: Mexico City (Juan Pablos, 1539), Goa in India (1556), Cambridge, Massachusetts (Stephen Daye's press, Bay Psalm Book 1640)
The Ottoman Empire: İbrahim Müteferrika's press for Ottoman Turkish books (opened 1727, first book 1729), though Jewish, Armenian and Greek communities had presses earlier
keyFacts: The Relation of 1605 is recognized by the World Association of Newspapers as the first newspaper
The Bay Psalm Book (1640) was the first book printed in British North America
The Statute of Anne gave a 14-year term, renewable once
outline.hook: For 350 years printers pulled wooden presses by hand — then came iron, steam and the Industrial Revolution.

outline.title: Steam, Iron and Endless Paper
covers: The all-iron Stanhope press (about 1800) prints bigger sheets with less effort
Friedrich Koenig's steam-powered cylinder press, first used to print The Times of London on 29 November 1814
Richard March Hoe's rotary press (1840s) and William Bullock's web press (1863) printing on long continuous rolls of paper; Bullock died in 1867 after an accident with one of his presses
The papermaking machine: Louis-Nicolas Robert's 1799 patent, developed in England by the Fourdrinier brothers and Bryan Donkin — making paper in continuous rolls
Paper from wood pulp (Friedrich Gottlob Keller, 1840s) replaces scarce rags, making paper very cheap
Results: cheap 'penny papers', magazines, serialized novels (like Charles Dickens's), and mass schooling with textbooks
keyFacts: Koenig's press printed about 1,100 sheets per hour in 1814, several times faster than a hand press
Rotary presses by the late 1800s could print tens of thousands of sheets per hour
Keller's wood-grinding method dates to 1844
outline.hook: Presses were now lightning fast — but setting the type was still done by hand, one letter at a time, and pictures were hard to print.

outline.title: Typesetting Machines and Printed Pictures
covers: Alois Senefelder invents lithography (around 1796): drawing with greasy crayon on stone, using the fact that oil and water repel each other
Chromolithography and colorful posters, labels and cards in the 1800s
Ottmar Mergenthaler's Linotype (first used at the New York Tribune in 1886) casts a whole line of type ('line o' type') from a keyboard
Tolbert Lanston's Monotype (patented 1887) casts single letters, good for books
Halftones: turning photos into tiny dots of different sizes — the New York Daily Graphic printed an early halftone photo in 1880
Effects: huge newspapers with photographs, mass advertising, comics, and new jobs (and lost jobs) for typesetters
keyFacts: A Linotype operator could set type several times faster than a hand compositor
Halftone images look smooth because your eye blends dots too small to notice
Lithography means 'stone writing' in Greek
outline.hook: Senefelder's oil-and-water trick was about to become the backbone of almost all modern printing.

outline.title: How Modern Printing Works
covers: Offset lithography: discovered around 1903–1904 when Ira Washington Rubel found an image transferred from the rubber blanket printed more clearly; ink goes from plate to rubber blanket to paper
The science of offset: plates have image areas that attract oily ink and non-image areas that hold water and repel it
Four-color (CMYK) printing: cyan, magenta, yellow and black halftone dots combine to make full-color pictures (subtractive color explained simply)
Other methods: flexography (packaging), gravure (engraved cylinders for long runs), screen printing (T-shirts)
Chester Carlson invents xerography in 1938; the Xerox 914 copier (1959) makes copying fast
Gary Starkweather's laser printer at Xerox PARC (1971); home inkjet and laser printers in the 1980s (e.g. HP LaserJet, 1984) — how static electricity and toner, or tiny ink droplets, form letters
keyFacts: Carlson's first xerographic copy read '10-22-38 Astoria' (22 October 1938)
Modern web offset presses can print tens of thousands of newspapers per hour
Inkjet printers fire droplets measured in picoliters (trillionths of a liter)
outline.hook: Printing had become fast, colorful and everywhere — but all that power also brought serious problems.

outline.title: The Dark Side of Print
covers: Censorship and book burnings, e.g. the Nazi book burnings of 10 May 1933; banned books and jailed printers
Propaganda and fake news: printed lies, hate pamphlets, and hoaxes like the Great Moon Hoax in the New York Sun (1835)
Health dangers: lead poisoning in type foundries and print shops; toxic solvents and inks
Environment: trees, water and energy used for paper; chemical bleaching; recycling paper as a solution
Acid paper (roughly 1850–1980) slowly turning brittle and yellow in libraries, and efforts to save these books
Jobs lost to machines (scribes, later hand compositors, later Linotype operators) and fights over copyright and piracy
keyFacts: Acidic wood-pulp paper can crumble within decades; acid-free paper can last hundreds of years
Paper is one of the most recycled materials; fibers can usually be recycled several times (often quoted as about 5–7)
The Great Moon Hoax claimed in 1835 that life had been seen on the Moon
outline.hook: Then computers arrived, and printing began to leave paper behind altogether.

outline.title: From Desktop to Digital Publishing
covers: Phototypesetting replaces hot metal type in the 1960s–1970s
Michael Hart starts Project Gutenberg in 1971 by typing up the US Declaration of Independence — the first free e-book library
Desktop publishing (1985): Apple Macintosh, Apple LaserWriter, Aldus PageMaker and Adobe's PostScript language (John Warnock and Charles Geschke) let anyone design pages
Tim Berners-Lee invents the World Wide Web (proposal 1989, first website 1991) — anyone can publish to the whole world
E-readers and e-ink (Sony Reader 2006, Amazon Kindle 2007), e-books, blogs, print-on-demand and self-publishing
Digital libraries and archiving (e.g. the Internet Archive, founded 1996) — and the challenge of keeping digital files readable for centuries
keyFacts: Project Gutenberg began on 4 July 1971 and now has tens of thousands of free e-books
The first website went online in 1991 at CERN
Printed books are still sold in very large numbers alongside e-books
outline.hook: Printing now means words on screens — but the newest printers are not printing words at all.

outline.title: The Future of Printing — and the Big Picture
covers: 3D printing: Chuck Hull's stereolithography (patent filed 1984, granted 1986) builds objects layer by layer; uses today from toys to rocket parts
Bioprinting (living cells for research tissues), printed electronics, flexible screens and electronic paper
Will paper survive? Printed books, libraries and paper next to screens and AI-written text
Big lessons: inventions are built on earlier inventions (clay, paper, woodblocks, metal type, presses, computers), credit is shared across many cultures
Why copying words matters: freedom of speech, learning, science and memory — and the responsibility to publish truthfully
Tie the journey together from Uruk's clay tablets to the reader's own screen, inviting the reader to become a publisher too
keyFacts: 3D printers make objects by adding thin layers, often a fraction of a millimeter thick
Writing is about 5,000 years old; printing with movable type in Asia about 1,000 years old; Gutenberg's press over 570 years old
Bioprinted tissues are used in research; printing whole working human organs is not yet possible
outline.hook: End by reminding readers that every page they read — paper or screen — is the latest step in a 5,000-year story they can now add to.

glossary: cuneiform — wedge-shaped writing pressed into clay, first used in Sumer
papyrus — a writing material made from pressed strips of a reed plant; not true paper
parchment / vellum — writing material made from specially prepared animal skin (vellum is fine calfskin)
codex — a book with pages bound on one side, like books today
paper — a thin sheet made from plant fibers beaten in water, scooped onto a screen and dried
woodblock printing — carving a whole page in reverse on wood, inking it and pressing paper on it
movable type — separate pieces for each character that can be arranged, printed and reused
punch — a steel rod with a letter carved backwards on its tip, used to make a matrix
matrix — a piece of copper with a letter-shaped dent, used as the mould for casting type
type metal — an alloy of lead, tin and antimony used to cast metal type
compositor — the worker who sets type into lines and pages
forme — the locked-up pages of type ready to be inked and printed
platen — the flat plate in a press that pushes paper against the inked type
incunabula — books printed in Europe before 1501 ('cradle books')
lithography — printing from a flat surface using the fact that oil and water repel each other
offset printing — ink goes from a plate to a rubber blanket and then onto paper
halftone — a picture made of tiny dots of different sizes that the eye blends into shades
CMYK — cyan, magenta, yellow and black, the four inks used for full-color printing
xerography — copying with static electricity and powdered toner (how photocopiers and laser printers work)
3D printing — making a solid object by adding material one thin layer at a time
doNotSay: Do not say Gutenberg invented printing or movable type first — woodblock printing (China), ceramic movable type (Bi Sheng, 1040s) and metal type (Korea) came earlier
Do not say the Gutenberg Bible was the first printed book — the Diamond Sutra (868) and Jikji (1377) are older, and Mainz printed smaller items before the Bible
Do not say Cai Lun invented paper from nothing — older paper fragments exist; he improved and promoted it
Do not call papyrus 'paper' or say paper was invented in Egypt
Do not state as fact that Chinese prisoners from the Battle of Talas (751) brought papermaking west — it is a traditional story
Do not state as fact that parchment was invented at Pergamon because of a papyrus ban — it is a legend
Do not state as fact that Laurens Coster printed before Gutenberg — it is a legend
Do not say Gutenberg got rich or famous in his lifetime — he lost much of his business to Fust and was never wealthy
Do not give Gutenberg an exact birth date — it is unknown (around 1400)
Do not say Gutenberg invented the screw press — he adapted presses already used for wine, oil and paper
Do not state as certain that Luther hammered the Ninety-five Theses onto the Wittenberg church door — historians debate it; what is certain is that they were printed and spread quickly
Do not say everyone in the Middle Ages was illiterate or that the period was simply a 'Dark Age' with no learning
Do not say the printing press alone caused the Renaissance, Reformation or Scientific Revolution — it was a powerful helper among many causes
Do not give an exact number of surviving Gutenberg Bibles other than 'about 49' (complete and partial)
Do not say 3D printers can already print working human organs for transplant
Do not invent quotes; do not attribute famous lines (e.g. 'eighth wonder of the world' about the Linotype) to specific people without a reliable source
